'''Michael Duryea Williams''' (born 1957) is an American physicist, professor at [[Clark Atlanta University]], and current president of the [[American Vacuum Society|AVS: Science and Technology of Materials, Interfaces, and Processing]] (formerly [[American Vacuum Society]]). He is the first African American president of AVS.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=AVS Presidents: Past & Present |url=https://avs.org/about-avs/roster/presidents/ |access-date=15 May 2023 |website=AVS.org}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Williams was born in [[Dothan, Alabama]], and attended [[Dothan High School (Dothan, Alabama)|Dothan High School]].<ref name=":4">[https://www.proquest.com/historical-newspapers/morehouse-student-gets-fleischman-scholarship/docview/491452195/se-2 "Morehouse student gets fleischman scholarship."] (November 2, 1975). ''[[Atlanta Daily World]]''.</ref>

Williams attended [[Morehouse College]] and the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]] in [[Atlanta|Atlanta, Georgia]], for his undergraduate studies. He received dual bachelor's degrees in 1979, with a B.S. in physics from Morehouse College and a B.S. in nuclear engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=March 17, 2023 |title=Officers of the Society |url=https://avs.org/about-avs/roster/officers/michael-d-williams/ |access-date=March 17, 2023 |website=AVS}}</ref> While at Morehouse College, Williams received the Max C. Fleishman scholarship and was a member of the [[Society of Physics Students]] and the [[Atlanta University Center]] photography club.<ref name=":4" />

He then went on to earn a master's degree and PhD in physics at [[Stanford University]] in [[Palo Alto, California]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2014-11-21 |title=Three African American Taking on New Administrative Duties |url=https://www.jbhe.com/2014/11/three-african-american-taking-on-new-administrative-duties/ |access-date=2023-03-17 |website=The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education}}</ref> His thesis at Stanford was titled "The Effect of Chemical Reactivity and Charge Transfer on Gallium-Arsenide (110) Schottky Barrier Formation."<ref name=":6">Williams, M. D. (1987). ''[https://www.proquest.com/dissertations-theses/effect-chemical-reactivity-charge-transfer-on/docview/303637217/se-2 The Effect Of Chemical Reactivity And Charge Transfer On Gallium-arsenide (110) Schottky Barrier Formation]'' (Order No. 8707763). Available from ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global. (303637217).</ref> His doctoral advisor was [[William E. Spicer]] and he received his PhD in 1987.<ref name=":0" /> His co-advisor was [[Arthur Leonard Schawlow|Arthur Schawlow]], and he also studied under professors [[Ingolf Lindau]], Piero Pianetta, C. Robert Helms and Walter Harrison while at Stanford.<ref name=":6" />

== Career ==
Following graduation, Williams completed an appointment as a visiting scientist at [[IBM Research|IBM's Almaden Research Center]] in [[San Jose, California]], and subsequently began working at the Optoelectronics Research Department of [[Bell Labs|AT&T Bell Laboratories]] (now [[Bell Labs]]) in 1987.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Spring Research Seminar: Surface Physics and Semiconductors |url=https://calendar.kennesaw.edu/event/spring_research_seminar_surface_physics_and_semiconductors |access-date=2023-05-15 |website=Kennesaw State University |language=en}}</ref>

In 2002, Williams became chair of the Committee on Minorities of the [[American Physical Society]]. The COM bestows the annual [[Edward Bouchet|Edward A. Bouchet]] Award, and Williams also organized a session titled "The New Face of Physics," which included discussions on the demographics of minorities in physics.<ref>{{Cite news |first=Richard M. |last=Todaro|title=Focus on Committees |url=http://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200204/committees.cfm |date=April 2002|access-date=2023-03-17 |work=APS News |publisher=American Physical Society |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Committee on Minorities in Physics |url=http://www.aps.org/about/governance/committees/commin/index.cfm |access-date=2023-03-17 |publisher=American Physical Society|language=en}}</ref>

Williams joined the faculty at [[Clark Atlanta University]] in 1994, where he teaches currently.<ref name=":1" /> He began as an associate professor of physics and director of the Center of Excellence in Microelectronics and Photonics.<ref name=":2">[[Ronald E. Mickens|Mickens, Ronald]] (1999). ''[https://radar.auctr.edu/islandora/object/cau.ir%3A1999_mickens_ronald_e The African American Presence in Physics]''. Atlanta, Georgia: [[National Society of Black Physicists]]. p.&nbsp;73.</ref> He is professor and chair of the physics department and director of the Center for Excellence in Materials Physics (CEMP) at Clark Atlanta University.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Physics Research Centers |url=https://www.cau.edu/school-of-arts-and-sciences/physics/research-centers.html |access-date=2023-05-09 |publisher=Clark Atlanta University}}</ref> He is also a member of Clark Atlanta's Faculty Research Council.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The CAU Research Council |url=https://www.cau.edu/research-sponsored-programs/research-council.html |access-date=2023-05-09 |publisher=Clark Atlanta University}}</ref>

Williams has been a part of numerous professional organizations throughout his career, including AVS and the American Physical Society. He is also a member of [[Sigma Pi Sigma]], [[Beta Kappa Chi]], and [[Sigma Xi]] honor societies, and served on the [[National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences’]] Board of Army Science and Technology study committee for a review of directed energy technology.<ref name=":5" />

In 2014, Williams was elected to the board of directors of the [[American Vacuum Society|AVS]].<ref name=":1" /> Previously, he served in AVS roles including director, trustee, liaison to the AIP Liaison Committee on Under-represented Minorities, executive officer for the electronics materials and processing division, chair of the AVS diversity and inclusion committee, chair of the AVS chapters, divisions and groups (CDG) committee and chair of the governance committee.<ref name=":0" /> In 2021, he became an AVS fellow, and in 2022 was the society's president-elect. In 2023 he began his term as AVS president.<ref name=":5" /> Upon becoming president, Williams became the first African American person to lead AVS.<ref name=":3" />

== Research ==
Williams' research has focused on "achieving a fundamental understanding of the physical processes, growth morphology, interfacial strain and electronic structure modifications that occur at the surfaces and interfaces of epitaxially grown films and semiconductors," as well as the processing and growth morphology of 2-D metal dichalcogenides.<ref name=":0" />

Williams developed a free-standing [[quantum well]] (FSQW) for use in laser technology, and was awarded a patent for this concept.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Williams |first=M. D. |date=1996-11-01 |title=Free Standing Quantum Wells |journal=APS Southeastern Section Meeting Abstracts |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1996APS..SES..CC06W |pages=CC.06|bibcode=1996APS..SES..CC06W }}</ref>
